articles.title: 36 Hours in Naples, Fla.
articles.abstract: This small Gulf-side city has a pleasingly anodyne quality that’s worlds away from the cosmopolitan bustle found in Miami.

articles.title: 36 Hours in Naples, Fla.
articles.abstract: THIS city -- named after the one in Italy because of its beautiful bay -- is most widely known for its sugar-sand beaches, warm winter weather and sprawling, high-gated communities that attract older, well-off snowbirds who live to golf but go to bed early. (It has the nation's second highest number of golf holes per capita, just behind Myrtle Beach, S.C.). But now Naples is starting to draw a younger, more dynamic crowd attracted to outdoorsy pursuits off the course, high-end shopping and late-night noshing -- all in a laid-back, upscale setting with enough cultural interest to support more than 130 art galleries and a symphony orchestra.   MEGHAN McEWEN    Friday    5 p.m.  1 -- Goodnight, Sun    Drop off your bags and head straight to Naples Pier in time for the sunset -- an impressive show that beckons tourists and Neapolitans alike; some tote lawn chairs and coolers to the beach below. Last rebuilt in 1960 and strong enough to withstand Hurricane Wilma in October, the landmark extends 1,000 feet over the Gulf of Mexico, which teems with snapper, grouper and shark. (Note the signs warning fishermen not to clean their fish over the water.) As you wait for the applause-generating daily masterpiece and watch the pelicans dive for their dinner, keep an eye out for the occasional dolphin.    7 p.m.  2 -- Tiger Vision    ''The wild is wilder after dark'' is the tag line for the Naples Zoo's most unusual attraction: a nighttime tour using night-vision goggles. During the roughly two-hour tour, said to be the only one of its kind in the United States, the zoo director, David Tetzlaff, will personally guide you past African wild dogs, tigers, porcupine pens, lion dens, antelopes and monkeys. Do plan: tours are given on select nights during the winter, and tickets ($70 a person) tend to sell out (1590 Goodlette-Frank Road, 239-262-5409).    9 p.m.  3 -- Naples, as in Italian    While much of Naples's sprawling commercial development takes the form of the ubiquitous Florida strip mall, it's a rare gem like Naples Tomato (14700 Tamiami Trail North, 239-598-9800) that does something different inside. Opened by two New Hampshire transplants, Jack and Nadine Serfass, this new warehouse -inspired Italian-American restaurant prepares sweet, chunky sauce from heirloom tomatoes harvested locally. Never will you feast on better lasagna ($18.95), and the alder wood-plank Everglades tilapia ($29.95), topped with grilled tomato and truffled balsamic vinaigrette, is local seafood at its best.    Saturday    10 a.m.  4 -- Be One With Nature    Only three years old, Naples Botanical Garden (4820 Bayshore Drive, 239-643-7275) is in the opening stages of grand plans to develop its 160 acres into a plant paradise. The focus now is on botanicals along the 26th latitude (where Naples is), like reptilian-looking climbing oleander from West Africa and giant squill from Zanzibar. Grab a colorful butterfly identification guide at the entrance to the butterfly pavilion and try to find each wing design as you walk through the screened-in area. If you're comfortable with critters, proceed to the sections dedicated to geckos and to brightly colored chirpy honeycreepers and lorikeets, birds that aren't afraid to land on shoulders -- especially Beeper, nicknamed for his ability to mimic cellphone rings.    1 p.m.  5 -- Under the Banyan Tree    With winter temperatures hovering from the mid-70's to the low 80's, alfresco dining is the thing among Naples's tanned socialites. There are dozens of places for it, often with heat lamps at tables for cooler evenings. But the best outdoor patio in town may be the rustic courtyard at Campiello (1177 Third Street South, 239-435-1166), with its giant banyan tree and a stone fountain. The lunch menu, featuring classic thin-crust pizzas fired to Neapolitan perfection in a wood oven ($12.50) as well as a muffuletta piled high with capicolla, mortadella, soppressata, salami and provolone ($12.50), won't disappoint.    3 p.m.  6 -- A Good Segue    Naples has its share of interesting historical tidbits, which you can encounter during Naples Water and Land Tours' new one-hour Segway Tour (1000 10th Avenue South at the Charter Club Resort, 239-793-7529; $50). You'll have a hoot zipping up and down the tree-lined streets while fascinated passersby honk and holler as the guide gives a general introduction to the downtown area. Starting near the City Docks and bypassing the main commercial avenues, you'll see ''cracker houses'' -- the late-19th-century cottages of the area's first white settlers -- and Tin City, an old maritime market that has grown into a touristy outpost peddling T-shirts, gator heads and coral necklaces. Don't be fooled by President Bush's Segway spill; the 15-minute introductory course beforehand has successfully trained participants ages 5 through 92.    4:30 p.m.  7 -- The Greenback District    Sure, there are brand-new Tiffany and Gucci stores at the Waterside Shops at Pelican Bay, and Hermès and Vuitton shops are on the way. But you may prefer to skip the chain stores for the boutiques and art galleries of Fifth Avenue South and Third Street South downtown. After all, Marissa Collections (1167 Third Street South, 239-263-4333) is a 10,000-square-foot bastion of luxury that sells an impeccable collection of Versace, Prada, Zac Posen, Derek Lam, Vera Wang, Miu Miu, you name it. Marissa Hartington, who opened the store 30 years ago with $500, still handpicks each piece, steadily expanding the ''boutique'' section of trendier, more affordable labels because of a younger clientele. If it's art you're interested in, Broad Avenue South goes by the moniker Gallery Row. Representing the likes of Milton Avery and Wolf Kahn, the Marianne Friedland Gallery (359 Broad Avenue South, 239-262-3484) stands out as a spare and serious modern and American contemporary gallery amid blocks of more ornate, decorative works and old masters.    8 p.m.  8 -- Not an Early Bird Special    If the late-night dinner crowds at trendy restaurants like Blu Sushi and Café & Bar Lurcat aren't convincing enough that there's a younger vibe in town, then make a reservation at Nektar (849 Seventh Avenue South, 239-435-1882). The ultrasleek bright-orange Mediterranean-style restaurant was opened last year by two Albanian brothers, Armand and Elton Alikaj, who moved from New York and London respectively. Start with the daily soup ($8) -- a zesty lentil on one visit -- or the watermelon salad ($12) sprinkled with red onions, fresh Greek feta and mint. Based on old family recipes (their mom is in the kitchen each day), the entrees range from a lusty pork stew over fresh vegetable couscous seasoned with Moroccan spices, raisins and sun-dried tomatoes ($22) to a slow-roasted lamb shank au jus with braised fennel and potato purée ($29).    Sunday    8 a.m.  9 -- Natural Habitat    The Naples area has nearly 20 miles of groomed beaches. But Delnor-Wiggins Pass State Park (11100 Gulfshore Drive, 239-597-6196) is different. It is one of the last remaining natural barrier-island beaches in Naples -- a one-mile stretch from which you won't see any tall buildings, and where the ungroomed sand is strewn with shells and seaweed. Get there early (official opening, 8 a.m.) for flawless sand dollars, lightning whelks and cockle shells. You can rent a kayak at the concession stand, Hurricane Charlie's (239-314-0110), for a full ($30) or half day ($20). Paddle through the peaceful estuaries and mangroves -- a haven for dolphins, sea turtles, shore and marsh birds, as well as manatee, often spotted feeding in the sea grass beds during winter.    Noon  10 -- Wacky Racers    Three weekends a year -- the first was late last month, the next is March 4 and 5 and then Oct. 28 and 29 -- scruffy racetrack regulars and V-neck-sweater-wearing Palm Beach types come together for some down-and-dirty fun at the Mile o' Mud at Florida Sports Park (8250 Collier Boulevard, 239-774-2701), the last legal place to watch swamp buggy races in the country. Loud, oversize and odd-looking buggies tear around a soupy track, spitting mud and dipping into mushy sink holes, while whooping fans, crowded onto rickety metal and wooden bleachers, go absolutely berserk. Every season, the lucky lass crowned Swamp Buggy Queen is dunked in the mud as part of the finale celebration.    THE BASICS  Where Night Owls Join Early Birds       Most major airlines fly into Southwest Florida International Airport in Fort Myers, and Delta flies into the Naples Municipal Airport, which serves mainly private jets. Either way, you'll want to rent a car for your stay.     The Ritz-Carlton, Naples (280 Vanderbilt Beach Road, 239-598-3300; www.ritzcarlton.com) is right on the beach, featuring 450 rooms, access to the Greg Norman-designed Tiburon golf courses, and an extravagant pool and deck area. Rooms are $249 to $1,049, starting at about $650 in peak season but dropping in the off-season.     The Inn on Fifth (699 Fifth Avenue South, 239-403-8777; www.innonfifth.com) is a charming boutique hotel in the heart of Old Naples. Its 87 rooms are $150 to $400, depending on season.

articles.title: 36 Hours in Grand Forks, N.D.
articles.abstract: NORTH DAKOTA in the winter -- cold, you betcha. But in Grand Forks, a town of about 50,000 closer to Winnipeg than it is to Minneapolis, winter is not a forbidding season. There's plenty to do outdoors if you're up for it, but because Grand Forks is home to the University of North Dakota and its more than 13,000 students, there's a surprising number of things to do indoors as well. The people are remarkably friendly, perhaps the result of working together to hold back the Red River of the North, which last flooded in 1997 and would have destroyed the city were it not for the legions of hyperorganized volunteer sandbaggers. And while a majority of the inhabitants trace their ancestry to Norway or Germany, the Forks has grown more diverse with the increasing number of university students from overseas. Finally, consider the joke that Grand Forks played on Dave Barry when he ridiculed the city's efforts to promote tourism. Lured to the Forks by a postcard-writing campaign, he was the guest of honor at an official ceremony in 2002-- in which a municipal sewage pump station was named after him. The plaque at the site reads ''Dave Barry Lift Station No. 16.''   NEAL KARLEN    Friday    4 p.m.  1 -- Add the Pickle    Check in to the Hilton Garden Inn Grand Forks (4301 James Ray Drive, 701-775-6000) on the campus of the University of North Dakota and enjoy a swim and a hot tub. Then go to the lobby bar and get a bloody mary ($3.75), which will come with a pickle, as is the custom in the upper Midwest. After you've eaten it, you can grab another pickle from the bar. If you're feeling peckish for something warm that you can have right away, frozen Hot Pockets are available at the front desk for $2. It might make Conrad Hilton roll over in his grave, but the person at the check-in counter will smilingly volunteer instructions for heating them in your room's microwave.    5:30 p.m.  2 -- The Eiger Sanction    If you want a fine dining experience, a terrific choice is Sanders 1907, named after Sander Johnson, who built the original two-story warehouse in 1907 (and whose granddaughter converted the first floor into a restaurant in 1982). That building was severely damaged in the Red River flood of 1997, but the restaurant has been rebuilt nearby (22 South Third Street, 701-746-8970). It's best to call ahead for reservations, not because they're so fancy-shmancy in this almost always laid-back town, but so seating times can be staggered to allow the chefs to devote full attention to a menu that includes Swiss Eiger steak (Sanders's name for prime rib), crab cakes, walleye and buffalo meat. Entrees run $15 to $31. And don't forget to check out the Dakota-length bar and Wild West pool room.    7:30 p.m.  3 -- Hockey Night in Grand Forks    In 1998, the University of North Dakota accepted a pledge of $100 million from Ralph Engelstad, an alumnus who owned a Las Vegas casino where he staged Third Reich dress-up parties on Hitler's birthday. Mr. Engelstad's donation was to endow construction of a lavish rink for the pride of the university athletic program, its hockey team. Two years later, when the university considered changing its Fighting Sioux nickname, Mr. Engelstad decided to fight the scourge of political correctness by threatening to halt work on the half-finished building. The university relented, and today the Ralph Engelstad Arena is perhaps the most beautiful college hockey rink in the world -- and the main attraction in Grand Forks on a winter weekend evening. Forget for a few hours that the late Mr. Engelstad's name is on the marquee and marvel at the granite-lined floors, halls and restrooms, 300 closed-circuit televisions, 48 luxury suites and perfect sight lines for around 11,000 shrieking fans who come to cheer the only big-time sport in the state. The West regional of the N.C.A.A. hockey tournament will be held there March 24 and 25 (www.theralph.com, 877-917-4689; tickets, $21.50).    10 p.m.  4 -- Casino Boreal    Grand Forks isn't Vegas, or even the Indian reservations with their slots-blackjack-and-poker palaces just across the river in Minnesota. But there are still plenty of places in town where you can legally drop a bundle by hitting on 16 while playing 21 or buying too many bingo cards to keep track of at once. In Grand Forks, you'll find casinos in a variety of places (all run, according to state law, by nonprofit organizations, including the Greater Grand Forks Convention and Visitors Bureau): Big Daddy's Lounge, which is also an off-sale liquor store, (1405 DeMers Avenue, 701-775-7740); Dagwood's Bar and Grill, a saloon serving bar food (425 North 42nd Street, 701-772-8044); or Charlie Brown's Casino, which has three tables for blackjack and about 200 seats for bingo (414 Gateway Drive, 701-772-7620).    Saturday    9 a.m.  5 -- After the Whiteout    The convention and visitors bureau calls the area a ''winter wonderland,'' which is one way to think of the eight blizzards whose snowmelt led to the great flood of April 1997. Still, there's terrific snowshoeing and cross-country skiing in Grand Forks, and only a weenie wouldn't go outside. The best venues are the Greenway, which runs alongside the Red River, including loops of groomed trails at Lincoln Drive Park -- or on the frozen river itself. For ski rentals, as well as directions, contact University of North Dakota Lifetimes Sports Center (701-777-3981) or one of the several other sports shops.    1 p.m.  6 -- Drawing on Disaster    The North Dakota Museum of Art (261 Centennial Drive on the University of North Dakota campus, 701-777-4195; www.ndmoa.com), shows contemporary work and has a fine collection of contemporary American Indian art. The first of a three-part exhibition of the museum's holdings runs to March 12. This show highlights 11 artists from locales as diverse as Cuba, Notre Dame University in Indiana and the White Earth reservation in Minnesota. Included is art from Douglas Kinsey, whose usual theme is disaster, a defining topic on the Great Plains, represented by apocalyptic paintings, while Frank Bigbear Jr.'s drawing ''Dolly's Discothèque'' considers traditional Indian life assimilating into urban American culture.    3 p.m.  7 -- Empire of the Arts    Housed in the refurbished movie palace where Al Jolson and ''The Jazz Singer'' first brought talkies to Grand Forks, the Empire Arts Center (415 DeMers Avenue; 701-746-5500; www.empireartscenter.com) stages events that reflect the surprising eclecticism of local sensibilities. ''The Vagina Monologues'' played from Feb. 2 to 4, while the Miss Grand Forks Pageant will take place Feb. 19.    5:30 p.m.  8 -- North of the Border    Mexican Village (1218 South Washington Street, 701-775-3653) is Grand Forks's first restaurant serving south-of-the-border specialties. Yet a characteristically homey North Dakotan atmosphere prevails, as does a typically North Dakotan take on Mexican cuisine -- like the chicken burrito, which is served slathered with the kind of Midwestern homemade gravy that normally covers biscuits. An average dinner for two is about $16.    7:30 p.m.  9 -- Red River Symphony    The Greater Grand Forks Symphony Orchestra (701-777-3359, online at www.grandforkssymphony.org) is in its 97th season. A full 60-piece orchestra, it performs in various local venues, like the Empire Arts Center and the Alerus Center, a convention center large enough to stage Fighting Sioux football games. The symphony's next performance is March 9 at the Chester Fritz Auditorium on the university campus.    Sunday    9 a.m.  10 -- A Grill Named Sioux    In the land of family values, there is nothing like a hearty home-style breakfast at a 24-hour restaurant, the Big Sioux Cafe (4401 32nd Avenue South, 701-738-0441), which features lumberjack breakfasts that would fill Paul Bunyan and the Brawny Man together. The most popular item: the Trucker Special ($6.95), green peppers, onions, cheese, mushrooms, ham, bacon and sausage, all atop hash browns and the whole mélange crowned by two eggs.    Noon  11 -- Northern Air    Grand Forks Air Force Base, about 16 miles west of town, is home to the 319th Air Refueling Wing and its KC-135 Stratotankers, famed for their midair plane-to-plane refueling maneuvers. Even if you can't arrange a tour, you can see B-25, A-26 and B-52 bombers, an F-101 fighter and a Minuteman III missile, all used at one time at the base, out front. Call at least three weeks ahead to set up a tour (701-747-5023; public.grandforks.amc.af.mil/basetour.asp).    THE BASICS    Where Drinks Come With Pickles       Amtrak's Empire Builder train, which runs between Chicago and Seattle, stops twice a day in Grand Forks (800-872-7245, www.amtrak.com). Planes arrive at Grand Forks International Airport (701-795-6981, www.gfkairport.com) several times a day from Minneapolis on Northwest and its affiliated airlines. All major car rental agencies serve Grand Forks, as well as two taxi services: Nodak Radio Cab (701-772-3456) and Grand Forks Taxi (701-780-8890).     The Hilton Garden Inn Grand Forks, on the campus of the University of North Dakota, offers 100 rooms from $84 a night (4301 James Ray Drive, 701-775-6000; www.hiltongardeninn.com).      For a non-Hilton experience, try the 511 Reeves Bed and Breakfast, a converted 1901 Victorian mansion a block from the river. Though it has only three guest rooms, each bears a distinct personality: the wildlife-themed Audubon Room has noncreepy examples of taxidermy; the quaint Americana Room; and the wistful Cottage Room, meant to evoke images of childhood (511 Reeves Drive; 701-775-3585, www.bbonline.com/nd/511reeves; rooms are $89 to $99).

articles.title: 36 Hours in St. John, V.I.
articles.abstract: ASK a local for the address of a restaurant or store in St. John, the smallest, least developed and most beautiful of the three major United States Virgin Islands, and you'll probably get a blank stare. Even asking for the name of a road can leave St. Johnians scratching their heads.      There are practically no street signs, but that's O.K. because St. John -- about nine miles long and five miles wide -- is easy to get around. Everyone knows everyone and where everything is.

articles.title: 36 Hours in SoMa, San Francisco
articles.abstract: IF you visit the SoMa district of San Francisco, you can eat a five-course meal while you sit on an oversize bed and watch a performance artist stretch the definition of theater. You can drop in on a penguin feeding or paddle a kayak in search of floating baseballs in the bay. This stretch of the city south of Market Street, long known for its alternative art and music scene, has matured into a mix of trendy restaurants, gritty bars, swank hotels and warehouses reworked to stage live music. It has a bustling waterfront, a major league baseball stadium and engrossing museums. SoMa's character has been shaped by recent cycles of boom and bust. The district lost some of its edge during the frenzy of the late 1990's, as soaring rents shut down galleries and nightclubs and stock-inflated Internet start-ups moved in. When the high-tech bubble burst, SoMa's landscape shifted once again. Lofts languished vacant, and the well-to-do young people on Razor scooters vanished overnight. Lately, though, new life has sprouted. There is some scruffiness, and you can still duck into a club too cool to post its name above the door. But for all its youthful spirit, SoMa feels more grown-up -- not stodgy, but adult -- than ever, with family attractions by day and energy that lingers after dark.   JOSH SENS    Friday    5 p.m.  1 -- Sake and Sculpture    A split-level space with a split personality, Varnish Fine Art (77 Natoma Street, 415-222-6131) is a wine bar in the body of an art gallery. On Friday afternoons, a post-work crowd gathers, inspecting art installations while sipping pinot noir. Music pulses from the sound system, and house wines pour for $5 a glass. Put away a few sake cocktails (also $5, at happy hour) and you might wind up ordering a steel-and-blown-glass sculpture for $6,200. A few doors down, John Colins (90 Natoma Street, 415-543-2277) is another popular spot to wash away the workweek. The regulars here are younger than at Varnish. And louder. But the surfing films screened on the wall are silent. A bouncer guards the door, but the industrial-chic atmosphere is far from daunting.    8 p.m.  2 -- Dinner at Ame    After years of running Terra, an acclaimed restaurant in the Napa Valley, the husband-and-wife team of Hiro Sone and Lissa Doumani have set up a second shop, on the ground floor of the haute and happening St. Regis Hotel. Their new restaurant, Ame (pronounced Ah-MAY, 689 Mission Street, 415-284-4040), serves a selection of superb sashimi, crudo, ceviche and carpaccio, as well as entrees (thick grilled pork chop with Dijon verjus, $32) that smack of California by way of France. The dining room is elegant but relaxing, with plush seats and lighted silk sculptures that float overhead like underwater creatures. But the most coveted seats are at the sashimi bar. Request whatever sashimi they're serving, or the sake-marinated black cod with shrimp dumplings in shiso broth ($29.50), which deserves its standing as Mr. Sone's signature dish.    Saturday    9 a.m.  3 -- Pick Your Paddles    Grab coffee and house-made pastries at Town's End Restaurant & Bakery (2 Townsend Street, 415-512-0749), then stroll along the waterfront to Pier 38, where City Kayak (415-357-1010) launches its boats. The company's guided Bay Bridge tour ($59 a person) will take you on the water and underneath the bridge, San Francisco's other lovely but less famous span. Enjoy great views of the city before paddling out to McCovey Cove behind SBC Park (soon to be renamed AT&T Park), home field of the San Francisco Giants. You might recognize the cove as the splash-landing point for many a Barry Bonds home run. (It's named for a Giants slugger from an earlier day, Willie McCovey.) In April, when the baseball season gets under way, you can rent a kayak on your own (from $15 an hour, two-hour minimum) and join other boaters in a mad dash for a floating souvenir. Kayak lessons are included with the price of a guided tour. Tour schedules can vary, depending on the tides.    12:30 p.m.  4 -- A New Museum    Museumgoers familiar with the SF MoMa (the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art) have a new South of Market acronym to memorize: MoAD (685 Mission Street, 415-358-7200; admission is $8), for the Museum of the African Diaspora, which opened in December. It explores the cultural contributions made by people of African descent as they have spread around the world, through migrations forced and voluntary. Interactive exhibits touch on a range of topics from the influence of the slave trade on Brazilian cuisine to the African roots of Charlie Parker's jazz.    3:30 p.m.  5 -- Lunch of the Penguins    If emperor penguins, as portrayed in ''March of the Penguins,'' don't exactly have it easy, African penguins, as displayed at the Steinhart Aquarium (875 Howard Street, 415-321-8000; $7 admission), don't exactly have it rough. The penguins, whose natural home is off the coast of southern Africa, are fed twice daily (at 11 a.m. and 3:30 p.m.) by aquarium staff members, who dole out herring while educating visitors. The Steinhart's permanent home is across town in Golden Gate Park, but that site is being completely rebuilt. So the aquarium will remain in its temporary SoMa space until 2008.    5:30 p.m.  6 -- Cocktails at CoCo500    Classics like the mojito and the caipirinha join concoctions like the lemongrass bloody mary (lemongrass-infused vodka, tomato juice and sriracha chili sauce; $9) on the cocktail menu of CoCo500, a new SoMa restaurant (500 Brannan Street, 415-543-2222). It's almost always humming, but it's the house special drink, the CoCo500 cocktail (Thai basil, kaffir lime vodka, fresh lime; $10) that really generates a buzz.    7:30 p.m.  7 -- Dinner in Bed    Though it feels like a satire of ''Sex and the City,'' Supperclub San Francisco (657 Harrison Street, 415-348-0900) is actually a branch of a restaurant born in Amsterdam. ''Let's go to bed,'' the host says, whisking you into an all-white room with oversize beds laid out for 175. The prix-fixe menu ($70 on Saturdays) ranges widely, from baby back ribs to four-cheese ravioli with chives and lemon verbena oil. It can take up to three and a half hours to go through five courses. But there's no nodding off. Not with the eclectic artistic presentations, which can be music, film or a fashion show, to entertain you. Imagine a man clad in a diaper, climbing down a stairway while sucking on a pacifier. Those in the mood for a more traditional meal should try Town Hall (342 Howard Street, 415-908-3900), where the well-executed dishes draw on American regional influences and nobody eats lying down. Main courses, in the $20's, change often.    10 p.m.  8 -- Saturday Night Live    In keeping with the recent history of SoMa, Mezzanine (444 Jessie Street, 415-625-8880; www.mezzaninesf.com; admission $15 to $25), a cool live-music venue, occupies a warehouse once inhabited by a dot-com. It caters to all tastes: hip-hop, soul, world beat, jazz. Order a martini at one of the bars and feel as if you're in your own music video. Fatboy Slim, Martin Luther and the National have all played here. But don't expect anything too mainstream. Hootie & the Blowfish would be barred at the door.    Sunday    10 a.m.  9 -- Young Bliss    Bliss San Francisco (181 Third Street, on the fourth floor of the W Hotel, 415-281-0990) casts itself as the young person's spa, soothing but free of self-seriousness. It features rock and jazz, not New Age whale music. Grab a brownie as you await your treatment. The Hangover Herbie ($215) includes a revitalizing face mask and an ''antimigraine'' massage. There's really nothing different about the Manly-Cure ($23) treatment. It's just a more macho way of saying you had your nails done.    12 p.m.  10 -- Dim Summing    Dim sum fiends may debate where to get the best buns in San Francisco. But few would dispute the atmospheric appeal of Yank Sing (1 Rincon Center, 101 Spear Street, 415-957-9300). The restaurant stands in what was once a post office, an Art Deco building with colorful murals in the lobby. Order an imperial walnut salad ($7.30) and steamed pork buns ($3.65) and sip jasmine tea. If the spa didn't relax you, the indoor water shower, which spills gently from the ceiling and splashes in the atrium outside the restaurant, will.    Fish for Baseballs Or for a Good Time       The South of Market district of San Francisco is about a half hour from both San Francisco International Airport and Oakland International Airport. Bay Area Rapid Transit, or BART, runs from both airports to stops in downtown San Francisco a short walking distance from SoMa. Taxis from either airport cost $30 to $50.      St. Regis Hotel, San Francisco (125 Third Street, 415-284-4000) is a luxurious hotel that takes many of its aesthetic cues from the nearby San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. The hotel is home to Ame, one of the city's best new restaurants. The St. Regis's cool, contemporary accommodations include 260 guest rooms, starting at $379.     Beautiful bay views, a luxury spa and a penthouse-level yoga studio are some of the attractions of Hotel Vitale (8 Mission Street, 415-278-3700), on the revitalized Embarcadero waterfront. It has 199 rooms, $279 to $399.     Marriott Courtyard San Francisco Downtown (299 Second Street, 415-947-0700) features comfortable accommodations, combined with a convenient location just blocks from the ballpark and museums. Rooms start at $149.

articles.title: 36 Hours in Winston-Salem, N.C.
articles.abstract: WINSTON-SALEM is a place of peculiar juxtapositions. At cafes, immaculately coiffed Southern socialites sit beside pierced and tattooed students from the North Carolina School of the Arts, and an idle brick smokestack from a century-old R. J. Reynolds tobacco plant stands near a domed Cesar Pelli skyscraper that looks like a giant roll-on antiperspirant. You can go to an art museum in what was once a tobacco tycoon's mansion and you can take in Nascar races or visit a museum devoted to stock cars. The city -- known as the birthplace and home of Krispy Kreme Doughnuts -- has galleries that sell turned wood furniture and hand-stitched quilts. Winston-Salem (population 187,500), in the Piedmont region at the base of the Blue Ridge Mountains, was created in 1913 after the consolidation of the post offices of two adjacent small towns: Salem, founded in 1766 by the Moravian Protestant sect, and Winston, established in 1849 and named for a local Revolutionary War hero. Events like the National Black Theater Festival, held every two years, and the annual RiverRun International Film Festival attract tens of thousands -- but perhaps the biggest draw is the relaxed Southern sensibility, which makes it the kind of place where lingering over a sweetened iced tea is always encouraged.   KATE MURPHY    Friday    4 p.m.  1 -- Gallery Hopping    The city's downtown arts district (Trade Street between Fifth and Seventh Streets) has 16 galleries that emphasize regional talent. Stop by Piedmont Craftsmen (601 North Trade Street, 336-725-1516), which displays and sells the work of more than 350 top Southeast artisans, including hand-stitched quilts, turned and handmade wood furniture, pottery and blown glass. On the first Friday of every month, galleries are open to 10 p.m. for First Friday Gallery Hops.    7 p.m.  2 -- Soul Food    With its hardwood floors, dim lighting and paintings by local artists, Sweet Potatoes (529 Trade Street, 336-727-4844) is a far cry from the eyelet curtains and Formica lunch counters of a typical Carolina cafe. Order a fried-green-tomato-and-okra basket with sweet potato aioli ($6.95) or Carolina crab dip ($7.25) and maybe some ''Southernly'' fried chicken ($12.95) or drunken brandy pork chops ($13.95). Of course, there's sweet potato pie for dessert as well as chocolate pecan pie and sweet potato bread pudding (all $4.25).    9:30 p.m.  3 -- Local Beat    Listen to everything from ragtime to reggae at downtown clubs like Speakeasy Jazz (410 West Fourth Street, 336-722-6555; www.speakeasyjazz.net), which features jazz and mellow Latin bands and caters to a button-down, martini-drinking crowd. A few blocks away, the Garage (110 West Seventh Street, 336-777-1127; www.the-garage.ws) is more of an alt-rock, beer-in-a-plastic-cup type of place that draws students from Wake Forest University.    Saturday    9 a.m.  4 -- Pipin' Hot    Krispy Kreme Doughnuts got its start in 1933 when Vernon Rudolph bought the secret yeast-raised doughnut recipe from a chef from New Orleans. In 1937, he opened the first Krispy Kreme store in Winston-Salem, and the rest is sugar-glazed history. The company is still based in the city, and residents swear the doughnuts at the shop on the original site (259 South Stratford Road, 336-724-2484) are superior to those at the other 300-plus stores nationwide. Sit at one of the chrome-trimmed tables and watch the doughnuts travel on the shiny conveyor belt to fill your order. The neon Hot Doughnuts Now sign lights up when a fresh batch comes out of the oven.    10:30 a.m.  5 -- Tobacco Tales    Reynolda House (2250 Reynolda Road, 336-758-5150; $10 for adults, free under 18), the former country estate of the tobacco magnate R. J. Reynolds, is now a museum of American art. It is a restored 1917 mansion that is furnished as it was when the Reynolds family lived there, save for the art on the walls, which includes works by Gilbert Stuart, Frederic Church, Andrew Wyeth, Grant Wood and Georgia O'Keeffe. Don't miss the basement's bowling alley, shooting gallery and Art Deco-style bar -- or the 4 acres of formal gardens and 125 acres of fields and woodlands filled with fragrant magnolias and soft-needle pines. Have lunch on the patio at Simplyummy (122 Reynolda Village, 336-724-9779). The menu changes weekly but usually features fresh sandwiches like the village gobbler ($7.25), which is roasted turkey, havarti, tomato jam mayonnaise, baby spinach and shredded carrots on focaccia.    3 p.m.  6 -- Vroom Room    North Carolina is the spiritual home of stock-car racing, and Winston-Salem is home to the Winston Cup Museum (1355 North Martin Luther King Jr. Drive, 336-724-4557; $5 for adults). The museum contains a collection of racecars, drivers' suits, trophies and a photographic wall mural, which shows how Nascar has evolved. For example, as late as the 70's, drivers wore only lap belts for protection.    6:30 p.m.  7 -- Where There's Wood Smoke    You're in North Carolina, so you must have some wood-smoked Piedmont barbecue. The Original Little Richard's (4855 Country Club Road, 336-760-3457), a wonderfully ramshackle place with old license plates as wall décor and red-and-white-checked tablecloths, serves authentic chopped, coarse-chopped or sliced pork barbecue with slaw and hush puppies (starting at $4.59). Try the banana pudding ($1.59) and chocolate cream pie ($1.99) for dessert.    8 p.m.  8 -- Revving at the Raceway    To see cars tearing around a track rather than sitting spit-shiny in a museum, go to Bowman Gray Stadium (1250 South Martin Luther King Jr. Drive, 336-679-8118; admission $10), where races have been held for more than 50 years -- Nascar's longest-running weekly racetrack. The top level of cars at Bowman Gray are in the modified class; with their big tires and exposed engines, they look like 50's hot rods. It's just a quarter-mile loop, which means plenty of nail-biting action. The drivers are usually from the area and tend to have loyal followings. Prime racing season is April through August; this year it starts on April 29.    Sunday    10 a.m.  9 -- Restful Acres    Walk the paths through the emerald-green grounds of God's Acre, or Gottes Acker, a Moravian cemetery in the Old Salem area (at Church and Cemetery Streets) that is actually about 12.5 acres. The gravestones date to the 18th century and are all flat white marble slabs. The uniformity ensures that the observer cannot distinguish the rich from the poor. The dead are buried chronologically, ''in the order called by God,'' and divided by age, sex and marital status, according to Moravian tradition. On the Saturday before Easter, each plot is cleaned and decorated with fresh flowers so the cemetery looks like a giant colorful patchwork quilt.    Noon  10 -- Moravian Meal    At the Old Salem Tavern (736 Main Street, 336-748-8585), staff members in 18th-century costume serve meals in a building from 1816. The lunch menu includes traditional Moravian dishes like double-crusted chicken pie with sautéed vegetables ($7.50) and sauerkraut stew with braised beef and pork ($7.50).    1:30 p.m.  11 -- Living History    At the Old Salem Museums and Gardens (Main and Church Streets and Old Salem Road, 336-721-7350), a restoration of the church-governed Moravian town of the mid-18th through mid-19th centuries, craftspeople demonstrate trades like shoemaking and pottery making. The Old Salem Toy Museum and Museum of Early Southern Decorative Art are also on the grounds. An all-in-one ticket is $21 for adults.    3 p.m.  12 -- Farewell Folly    Körner's Folly (413 South Main Street, Kernersville, 336-996-7922; $6 for adults), 15 minutes outside Winston-Salem on the way to the airport, is the 22-room former home of Jule Körner, an artist and architect who painted Bull Durham cigarette ads on buildings throughout the South. It is a dizzying amalgam spread over three stories and seven levels; ceilings range from 5 to 25 feet. There are intricate mosaic tile on the floors, murals, trap doors and pivoting windows.    THE BASICS    Fast Cars, Tobacco And Doughnuts       Piedmont Triad International Airport, 25 minutes from town, is served by most major carriers. On weekdays, an express shuttle bus (www.partnc.org) will take you from the airport to downtown for $2. For exploring the city, you will want a rental car.      Most major hotel chains have operations in Winston-Salem, but there are nice boutique places to stay as well. The Brookstown Inn (200 Brookstown Avenue, 800-845-4262; www.brookstowninn.com) is in a converted cotton mill. Its 70 rooms have high ceilings, exposed brick, wood beams and reproduction antique furniture. Breakfast is included and is served in a quaint sunny dining room, and wine and cheese are served in the equally pleasant parlor in the evening. Rates range from $89 to $135.      Another option is the Augustus T. Zevely Inn (803 South Main Street, 800-928-9299; www.winston-salem-inn.com).The only inn in the Old Salem Historic District, it is a restored 19th-century brick house with rear L-shaped verandas upstairs and downstairs. There are 12 rooms, some with working fireplaces. Rates start at $95, which includes breakfast in a colonial-style dining room. Wine and cheese are offered in the parlor in the evening.

articles.title: 36 Hours in Lower Manhattan
articles.abstract: WELCOME to Lower Manhattan, you're already behind schedule. Was it really just a few years ago that people wondered if the area would ever recover? Since 9/11 the pace of development has only intensified (everywhere but ground zero, where the pace of stagnation has intensified). Thirty-six hours seems far too little time to cover it all. But it's a great start.   ARIEL KAMINER    Friday    3:30 p.m.  1 -- Hang Out    On a tiny platform 23 feet off the ground, every natural impulse tells you to stay away from the edge. But Jonah, a rather dreamy trapeze instructor, tells you to lean over it -- way over it -- and so you lean. Then he tells you to bend your knees and jump off. And so, against all reason, you jump. What follows is something close to flying, accompanied by the incomparable sensation of zoom and the sound, perhaps, of your own giddy scream. That first step is a doozy all right, but the odd collection of charming teachers at the Trapeze School of New York (Hudson River Park just south of Canal Street, 917-797-1872; www.trapezeschool.com; $57 for a two-hour beginner class, plus $22 registration fee) make it fun. The school sits right on the river, with peerless views of the Statue of Liberty and the skyline. What better way to situate yourself in Lower Manhattan than while hanging from your knees and swinging a 70-degree arc?    6 p.m.  2 -- Footing the Bill    Feel wobbly? Time for acupressure massage at the Fishion Herb Center (107 Mott Street, 212-219-1465; $35 an hour), a cramped warren of fluorescent-lighted cubicles that's far, indeed, from the Valrhona-chocolate facials of uptown spas. Settle into a cracked old wing chair while a Chinese masseur bears down on the tip of your fourth toe, or the area right inside your heel, tiny spots said to correspond to precise parts of the body. Check the laminated chart and note that he's put his hands on not only your ''liver'' and ''spleen'' but also places -- hello! -- not fit to name in a family newspaper. What's the standard tip for that?    8 p.m.  3 -- Bridge to the 19th Century    Depending on whom you believe, the Bridge Café (279 Water Street, 212-227-3344) may be the city's oldest drinking establishment, tracing its ancestry to 1794. It wears its history lightly, with a low-key New American menu and friendly setting (seared diver scallops, $26; lobster pot pie, $20). After dinner you can wander the almost ridiculously picturesque streets just south of the Brooklyn Bridge (but north of the dreaded South Street Seaport mall), cobblestone alleys right out of a Walt Whitman poem.    10 p.m.  4 -- Admission to the Bar    Lower Manhattan is also the seat of the city government, so fight the lure of yet another ''Law & Order'' rerun and go see the real thing in action. The gritty night session of New York Criminal Court, at 100 Centre Street, is open to the public, but applause and/or booing is strongly discouraged. Afterward, go to Forlini's (93 Baxter Street, 212-349-6789) to have a Scotch with the only team that always comes out on top: the lawyers. Or, take a short perp walk toward the Tombs, Lower Manhattan's very own jail, and find Winnie's (104 Bayard Street, 212-732-2384), a gloriously, garishly seedy dive bar where tough customers and painted ladies drink cocktails and sing karaoke into the morning.    Saturday    9 a.m.  5 -- Tai Chi Theater    Full-body exercise can be a great start to the day, especially when you're not the one doing it. Every morning in Chinatown's Columbus Park, old men, young students and graceful women of a certain age gather in their own little groups to perform tai chi. Whatever its spiritual or physical benefits, it makes for beautiful spectacle, with everyone moving in perfectly choreographed slow motion, as though performing water ballet on land.    11 a.m.  6 -- Vienna Goods    By Saturday night, Blaue Gans (139 Duane Street, 212-571-8880), an update on the classic Viennese coffee house, is a crowded scene restaurant. But at this hour it's peaceful, sunny and oh so European, from the newspapers dangling from a bentwood rack to the soccer match on the flat-screen TV to the counter filled with pastries expressing principled dissent from American diet trends. Order some Wiener schnitzel the size of Poland or Kaiserschmarren (what might have been called French toast before the Franco-Prussian War, $8) and enjoy the most elaborate coffee presentation since the days of the Habsburgs.    1 p.m.  7 -- Art and About    Big scary galleries and august museums may hardly take notice, but new cultural activity still thrives amid Lower Manhattan's condo sales offices. TriBeCa is sprinkled with galleries, among them apexart (291 Church Street, 212-431-5270), a small nonprofit space that emphasizes group shows with a political theme; Art in General (79 Walker Street, 212-219-0473), an old-timer by comparison that commissions work that might not find a home in other venues; and Ethan Cohen Gallery (18 Jay Street, 212-625-1250), which specializes in contemporary Chinese art. With a new $27 million federal grant for cultural programs in the area, more art -- and more condo sales offices -- are on the way.    5 p.m.  8 -- And Staten Island, Too    The more futuristic buildings that go up in this neighborhood, the more of its history gets unearthed. Workers in Battery Park recently struck on what may be the oldest structure on the island, mere blocks from where Santiago Calatrava's PATH station will soon rise. Take a peek. Then take a ride. Is there any greater cliché than a sunset ride on the Staten Island Ferry? No, and so what. Grab a beer at the snack bar and a spot on the bow and toast Lady Liberty standing among all the tribes she spawned: dudes in fake Gucci, biddies back from the Met and, on one recent visit, a lumbering Goth goddess hiding behind elaborate facial tattoos. (Ferries run 24 hours. Fare: free.)    9 p.m.  9 -- Downstairs, Upstairs    TriBeCa has more than its share of multistarred restaurants, but they're booked, expensive and awfully serious. Bouley has recently sprouted a much smaller, much less daunting offshoot, across the street and one flight up. Upstairs at Bouley Bakery (130 West Broadway, 212-608-5829), as it's called, features some of the same great cooking in a tiny and happily crowded little perch (entrees top out in the low $20's and the superb burger is just $12). Reservations aren't accepted, and the line can be long, but while you're waiting you can watch the action in the open kitchen, and while you eat you can literally look down on people who paid four times as much for their meals.    Midnight  10 -- Sofia on the Hudson    If you can choose only one Bulgarian hipster bar this weekend, Mehanata is the way to go. This freakish little hybrid is at Broadway and Canal (416 Broadway, one flight up, 212-625-0981), but at times it feels like a different country, or planet. The crowd is a mix of cute college girls, sullen artists and burly Eastern Europeans -- with the odd whirling dervish thrown in for good measure. As a D.J. spins something trendy, everyone drinks and dances, and soon enough the night slides over the edge into genuinely weird terrain. Food is available but in no way advisable.    Sunday    11 a.m.  11 -- Why Is It So Bright?    There's something about dancing tabletop with a band of crazed Bulgarian hedonists that changes a person -- but how, and for how long, it's best not to ask. Much better plan: brunch at Smorgas Chef on Stone Street, a pretty cobblestone lane in the financial district (53 Stone Street, 212-422-3500). Bring a stack of newspapers but do not read them. Instead, treat yourself to lobster eggs Benedict ($18), administer frequent doses of coffee and ignore the ringing in your head. It will subside eventually. It has to.    THE BASICS    An Urban Crawl On the Island's Tip       One of Lower Manhattan's newest hotels may also be its fanciest: the Ritz-Carlton New York, Battery Park (2 West Street, 212-344-0800; www.ritzcarlton.com) opened in 2002 at the southern tip of the island. Expensive, but who can put a price on Staten Island views? Weekend accommodations start at $295 a night.     On the other end of the spectrum, but not far away, is the Cosmopolitan Hotel (95 West Broadway, 212-566-1900; www.cosmohotel.com). The hotel offers budget accommodations, which for New York means it's not as mealy as you'd expect, and it's not as cheap as you'd like. Perfectly decent if unglamorous rooms start at $129.      Just a few blocks north of Canal Street, the Blue Moon Hotel (100 Orchard Street, 212-533-9080; www.bluemoon-nyc.com) is a strong reminder of the Lower East Side's immigrant past. This converted tenement has been updated -- somewhat -- so that each of the 22 rooms looks like an apartment a stylish young slacker inherited from his Great-Aunt Sadie. Though if she knew that rooms there start at $330 on weekends, she'd plotz.

articles.title: 36 Hours in Fayetteville, Ark.
articles.abstract: A fast-growing college town of 62,000 in the Ozark foothills, Fayetteville is flush with youth, culture and natural beauty -- especially in spring, when the redbuds and dogwoods are in bloom and the University of Arkansas students emerge to frolic in the warm weather. Get there before it's too hot to hike the lush, forested trails that braid the area. Stroll through the leafy campus and holler ''Woooooooooo, Pig! Sooie!'' at the 72,000-seat Reynolds Razorback Stadium (but beware: hotels are already booked for the fall football season). Soak up the atmosphere that entranced a young Bill Clinton. Then wind your way down lively Dickson Street, a former strip of dive bars that has gotten a good scrubbing.   JULIE BESONEN    Friday    5:30 p.m.  1 -- George's on My Mind    Introspection over a beer is unthinkable at the boisterous George's Majestic Lounge (519 West Dickson Street, 479-442-4226). Neither majestic nor a lounge, this wood-detailed beer garden with a retractable roof has anchored the Dickson Street music scene for four decades. There's always live music during the Friday happy hour ($5 cover). You might see the revered Cate Brothers, a soulful hometown band known for 70's hits like ''Union Man,'' inspiring everyone, including bearded scholars, to cut loose on the dance floor in broad daylight.    7 p.m.  2 -- Notes From Underground    Right off the late 19th-century town square is Hugo's (25 1/2 North Block Street, 479-521-7585), a speakeasy-like basement bistro open since 1977 and overburdened with antique mirrors, vintage portraits and commemorative presidential plates. Young families and spirited students, 99 percent of them in jeans, aren't shy when it comes to tackling the juicy bleu-moon burger ($6.25), catfish po' boy sandwich ($6.50), baskets of fries ($2.50) and homemade pecan pie ($2.95). And there is a respectable beer selection as well.    8 p.m.  3 -- Live From the Living Room    When you're invited into someone's house for a concert and served coffee and cookies during intermission, it's a cozy, one-of-a-kind evening. Mike Shirkey, host of ''The Pickin' Post'' on KUAF public radio, frequently presents established folk and bluegrass musicians, like Al and Emily Cantrell and Stacey Earle, on a stage in his club-size living room very near Hugo's. Called GoodFolk Productions (229 North Block Avenue, 479-521-1812; www.goodfolk.org; $10 cover), it's almost as intimate as someone singing softly in your ear.    Saturday    10 a.m.  4 -- Market on the Square    A lot of towns have a farmers' market, but the one looping around Fayetteville's square is uncommonly engaging. On one corner is a harpist and fiddler, on another a banjo player keeping time with a young country clogger whose hip attire and hairdo would not be out of place in Lower Manhattan. The homegrown produce for sale is not typical either: sheriff leeks, mediana spinach and baby greens with edible flowers. Dan Coody, the mayor of this blue town in what is currently a red state, regularly plants himself on the sidewalk, shaking hands with supporters and amiably scrapping with opponents.    11 a.m.  5 -- Young Love    In 1975, on a salary of $16,450, Bill Clinton, a young University of Arkansas law professor, rashly bought a brick bungalow in Fayetteville for $20,500. Why? Because his elusive girlfriend, Hillary Rodham, had made a passing remark on how pretty it was while he was driving her to the airport. When she returned to town, according to his autobiography, ''My Life,'' he said: ''Remember that little house you liked so much? I bought it. You have to marry me now, because I can't live there alone.'' The ceremony was in the living room, and a reproduction of her Victorian-style lace wedding dress is on display there today. So is early campaign memorabilia. The rest is history. Last October the Clinton House Museum (930 California Boulevard, 479-444-0066; $5) opened to the public.    12:30 p.m.  6 -- Pick Up the Red Phone    Sink your teeth into the smoky, meaty, glazed rack of ribs ($16.95) at Penguin Ed's B & B Bar-B-Q (230 South East Avenue, 479-521-3663). Find rapture in its batter-fried pickles ($2.59) and time-honored fried peach pie ($2.50). Penguin Ed's is in a cedar-lined shack with a tarred roof, and it has stuck with a tradition of having customers call in their orders from red phones at each table.    1:30 p.m.  7 -- Objets d'Ozark    Tired of traveling to regional arts-and-crafts shows to sell their work, several Ozark artists formed a collective and opened Heartwood Gallery (428 South Government Avenue, 479-444-0888) three years ago. Twiglike necklaces of copper and stained glass, crazily colorful knit caps, striking watercolors, pottery and handblown glass are some of the things you may be tempted to take home from the mountains.    2 p.m.  8 -- Library Envy    You'll need a card if you want to check out a book, but the Fayetteville Public Library (401 West Mountain Street, 479-571-2222; www.faylib.org) is worth checking out for its own sake. The $23.3 million building opened in 2004 and won the library of the year award from Library Journal last year. Through its sweeping windows you'll find unparalleled views of the mountainous landscape. There's also free wireless, a cafe, an all-embracing periodicals section (yes, this week's gossip rags!), a serene reading room, a genealogical collection, supercomfy chairs and a lot of children's programs.    4 p.m.  9 -- Bivouac on a Mountainside    The only Confederate cemetery in Arkansas (500 East Rock Street) didn't open until 1873. The 622 well-ordered and mostly unmarked graves belong to Confederate soldiers who were originally buried where they fell, at nearby battlefields and roadsides or in lonely hollows. Eight years after the war ended, locals were paid $1.40 to $2.50 for each body exhumed and delivered for reburial. It was a tidy sum back then, and though most people probably took the task seriously, historians today are skeptical about some of the remains in the quiet glade on East Mountain.    8 p.m.  10 -- A Taste of Arkansas    Sassafras (708 North College Avenue, 479-444-6992), run by the proprietor and chef Steve Jenkins, follows the national trend of using local seasonal ingredients. It's an inspired white-linen restaurant inside a pearl-gray house with a green awning. Sit a spell over a bourbon or a martini (this is the South -- the food doesn't come fast) and nibble on creative homemade bread and sherried crab and artichoke dip ($5). Relish the supple pork tenderloin ($17) or breaded chicken with Madeira cream sauce and garlic mashed potatoes ($14), a welcome twist on Southern-fried chicken.    Sunday    9 a.m.  11 -- High-Class Hash    Indeed, Fayetteville isn't just a biscuits-and-gravy town anymore. In the Mill District on the south side of town is the newish Maison des Tartes (481 South School Avenue, 479-521-1004), housed in an old chick hatchery. The lofty, modern space serves strong coffee ($1.59), exceptional pâté de campagne ($8.99) and hand-hacked corned-beef hash with eggs ($13.95). An old dray, antique farm-to-market carts and five-gallon canning crocks filled with redbud branches are on hand, just in case you forget you're in Arkansas.    11 a.m.  12 -- A Flashlight for a Cave    To really become acquainted with the Ozarks, spend a couple of hours hiking the rugged scenic trails of Devil's Den State Park (Route 170, West Fork; 479-761-3325; www.arkansasstateparks.com), 25 miles south of Fayetteville. Two spooky sandstone caves, Devil's Den and the Devil's Icebox, are open for self-guided tours. Don't forget a flashlight -- and watch out for bats.    THE BASICS    Ozark Spring       Downtown Fayetteville is about 30 minutes from the Northwest Arkansas Regional Airport in Bentonville. Renting a car is a good idea.     Collaring hotel reservations for Razorback football weekends in the fall is already a predicament. Spring weekends are more open. The most appealing accommodations are right on the University of Arkansas campus at the Inn at Carnall Hall (465 North Arkansas Avenue, 479-582-0402; www.innatcarnallhall.com), a rosy brick Colonial Revival structure built in 1905 as a women's dormitory and transformed into a 49-room inn in 2003. Weekend rates are $92 to $196.     The comfortable 235-room Radisson Hotel (70 North East Avenue; 479-442-5555, www.radisson.com/fayettevillear) is convenient to the town square. Nightly rates are $105 to $159.     About 15 minutes outside Fayetteville, in Johnson, is the pastoral Inn at the Mill (3906 Greathouse Springs Road, 479-443-1800; www.innatthemill.com), with 40 rooms and 6 suites dedicated to notable architects. The award-winning James at the Mill restaurant adjoins it. Rooms are $85 to $165.
